analysis.one_liner: Caps national greenhouse gas emissions and trades permits, funding consumer refunds, efficiency, and clean energy.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 219-212 on June 26, 2009, with 44 Democrats joining nearly all Republicans against it, but the Senate never voted and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set a nationwide limit on greenhouse gas pollution, shrinking it from 2012 through 2050, and let companies buy, sell, and bank permits to emit. Most permits would have been given away to utilities and heavy industry rather than sold. Money from the permits that were auctioned would have gone to households, especially low-income ones, as refunds for higher energy bills. It also required utilities to meet a rising share of electricity from renewables and efficiency, tightened building and appliance efficiency rules, funded green job training, and created aid for workers and industries hurt by the transition.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households benefit from lower long-term climate risk, monthly energy refunds for low-income families, per-capita rebates from auction proceeds, and lower utility bills from stricter building, lighting, and appliance standards. Clean-energy industries and workers gain guaranteed demand and training programs. Coal utilities, refiners, and energy-intensive manufacturers also gain, in the form of free permits and subsidies that cushion the cost of the cap.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households, clean-energy firms, and fossil utilities

how_it_helps.text: Caps greenhouse gas emissions from covered sources at 97% of 2005 levels in 2012, falling to 83% of 2005 levels by 2020, 58% by 2030, and 17% by 2050, with a federal registry to track emissions.

Creates a monthly cash Energy Refund for low-income households equal to the estimated loss in purchasing power from higher energy costs, plus per-capita tax refunds from auction proceeds deposited in a Climate Change Consumer Refund Account.
Requires large retail electric suppliers to meet a combined efficiency and renewable electricity standard rising to 20% of demand by 2020 and staying there through 2039.

Sets national building code efficiency targets (30% savings on enactment, 50% by 2014-2015), a national retrofit program, stricter appliance and lighting standards, and rebates to replace inefficient manufactured homes, wood stoves, and appliances.
Funds green job training partnerships, a Green Construction Careers demonstration project, and climate change adjustment assistance for workers displaced by the transition.

Gives the Commodity Futures Trading Commission authority over carbon allowance derivatives, requires energy derivatives to trade on regulated exchanges, and requires position limits and central clearing, to guard the new carbon market against speculation and manipulation.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers, coal-fired utilities, refiners, and energy-intensive manufacturers would bear the cost of buying permits or cutting emissions. Consumers would face somewhat higher electricity, heating, and fuel prices, though the bill routes refunds and free allowances back to households and industry to offset much of that. The cap also would have preempted state and regional cap-and-trade programs during 2012-2017.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy-intensive industry

drawbacks.text: Most emission allowances were to be handed out free to electric utilities, natural gas distributors, refiners, carbon capture projects, and energy-intensive trade-exposed industries, rather than auctioned, shrinking the revenue available for consumer rebates and concentrating the value of a public resource in incumbent companies.

Covered entities could satisfy up to 2 billion tons of their annual compliance with domestic and international offset credits, and the offset market for agriculture and forestry offsets is inherently hard to verify, which critics warned could undercut the actual emissions cap.

The bill would have prohibited states from running their own cap-and-trade programs for capped emissions during 2012-2017, overriding stricter state efforts already underway in California and the Northeast.

The renewable electricity standard counts efficiency savings toward the target, allows a $25-per-megawatt-hour alternative compliance payment, and credits existing hydropower upgrades, so the 20% figure is weaker than it sounds.
Household energy prices would rise before and alongside the refunds, and the refunds' adequacy depended on EPA estimates of purchasing-power loss.
The bill's border provisions threaten tariffs on imports from countries without comparable emissions limits, which trading partners and import-dependent industries opposed as a trade-war risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain was real: a declining national cap on the pollution driving climate change, paid for partly by consumers but largely refunded to them, especially low-income households, while efficiency standards cut bills independently. The trade-off is that to win votes, Congress diluted the design: permits were largely given away to the very industries being capped, offsets could substitute for up to 2 billion tons of real reductions, state programs were preempted, and the renewable target was softer than it appeared. It was a meaningful climate bill with significant concessions to concentrated interests, not a clean one.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 219-212 after a 33-25 committee vote, but after landing on the Senate calendar in July 2009 it was never brought up for a vote, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Introduced May 15, 2009, by Rep. Henry Waxman and referred to nine committees, with hearings on May 18, 19, 20, and 21.
The House Energy and Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported on a party-line 33-25 vote on May 21, 2009, and the remaining committees were discharged in June so the bill could reach the floor.
The House passed the bill on June 26, 2009, by a recorded vote of 219-212: 211 of 256 voting Democrats in favor and 44 opposed, versus only 8 of 178 Republicans in favor and 168 opposed.

The Senate received the bill on July 6, 2009, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on July 7, 2009, where it remained; no Senate committee reported it and no floor vote ever occurred before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal utilities, oil refiners, and other greenhouse gas emitters came out ahead: they avoided a national cap on their emissions, kept emitting for free, and avoided border and permit costs, while households got no refunds and no efficiency investments that a paid-for version would have delivered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Emitting industries that avoided the cap

for.name: Henry A. Waxman
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, held hearings, and steered it through committee markup, which reported it 33-25.

for.name: Edward Markey
for.role: Chair of the Energy and Environment Subcommittee and House floor manager
for.what_they_did: Co-authored the bill and managed it through House floor consideration.

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Publicly pressed House members to pass the bill and staked his first-year agenda on it.

against.name: 44 of 253 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, nearly all from coal, oil, and manufacturing districts.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Placed the bill on the Senate calendar but never scheduled it for a floor vote, prioritizing other legislation as the 60-vote threshold for ending debate made the bill's path untenable.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split sharply by party: 211 of 256 voting Democrats yes versus 8 of 178 Republicans, with 44 Democrats defecting, mostly from fossil fuel and manufacturing states.

industries.industry: Coal mining and coal-fired electric utilities
industries.note: The emissions cap would cut coal demand over time, but the bill gave utilities large free allowances, funded carbon capture and sequestration with allowances and a new $1 billion/year industry assessment, and set lenient performance standards for new coal plants, entrenching coal's role as a compensated compliance channel. Households pay for this cushion through higher electricity prices.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: Refiners and fuel importers were covered by the cap but received free allocations, small-business refiner protections, and compensatory allowances for non-emissive fuel uses, softening their losses while consumers absorbed the remaining price increase at the pump.

industries.industry: Renewable energy developers and efficiency contractors
industries.note: The 20% renewable and efficiency standard creates guaranteed demand for wind, solar, geothermal, and efficiency services, and allowance allocations fund state renewable programs, retrofits, and clean energy deployment. Lower bills and cleaner air benefit the public alongside the industry.

A multi-trillion-dollar permit and offset market creates trading revenue for financial firms, but the bill placed it under FERC and CFTC oversight with position limits and mandatory clearing, which cuts against purely speculative gains.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive, trade-exposed manufacturers (steel, cement, chemicals, glass)
industries.note: These industries faced the cap but received free emission allowance rebates based on output and, absent a global agreement, importers of competing foreign goods would have had to buy international reserve allowances, effectively a border tariff protecting them. The protection is paid for by consumers and risks trade retaliation.

A USDA-run offset program would pay farmers and foresters for sequestration and manure management, a new revenue stream, but the environmental integrity of agricultural offsets is difficult to verify and the bill relaxed biofuel and renewable biomass definitions favored by the industry.

Revised loan guarantees, a new federally owned Clean Energy Deployment Administration issuing loans and guarantees for clean energy projects, and green bond financing open federal credit support to new nuclear construction, with prevailing-wage requirements attached.

industries.industry: State and regional carbon programs (California, RGGI)
industries.note: The bill prohibited state cap-and-trade programs covering capped emissions during 2012-2017, overriding programs states had built, though it let holders exchange state-issued allowances for federal ones.
